dbl_biometrics.about: Signing in with your fingerprint or face is handled by Windows Hello on PCs that support it. If you never sign in that way, this turns the feature off so there is one less thing running in the background. It makes no real difference to frames. Only use it if you're sure, because you'll be back to typing your PIN or password each time.

win_ai.summary: Turns off Copilot and its taskbar button, and stops Recall from taking screen snapshots.
win_ai.about: Copilot is Microsoft's AI assistant, and Recall is a feature that takes snapshots of what is on your screen. This turns both off and removes the Copilot button from the taskbar. It's a privacy choice that won't change your frames. Turn it on if you don't use Copilot and would rather Windows didn't keep pictures of your screen.

app_remove.summary: Uninstalls about thirty preinstalled Microsoft apps like Weather, Tips and Solitaire.
app_remove.about: Out of the box, your PC comes with a long list of Microsoft apps you may never open. Running this once uninstalls about thirty of them, from Weather and Tips to Solitaire and Skype, for a cleaner Start menu and a little more free space. It won't change your frames. It's meant for players who know which apps they rely on, since Camera, Mail, Alarms and Phone Link go too, though each can be reinstalled from the Microsoft Store.

app_settings.summary: Opens the Apps page in Windows Settings so you can uninstall apps yourself.
app_settings.about: Sometimes you'd rather decide for yourself what stays on your PC and what goes. This simply opens the Apps page in Windows Settings, where you can go through your installed programs and uninstall the ones you don't want. Nothing changes until you remove something yourself. It works well as a final, hand-picked step after the other cleanup options.

win_telemetry.summary: Applies over 200 settings that cut data collection, animations and mouse acceleration.
win_telemetry.about: More than 200 Windows settings change at once here: most data collection and the tasks behind it are switched off, animations are reduced and mouse acceleration is removed. The result is more privacy and a quieter Windows in the background, though frames rarely change in a way you can measure. It's meant for players who know what they're changing. Expect your mouse to feel different at first, location to be off, Store apps to stop running in the background, and driver updates to become your job.

win_optimize.summary: Applies about fifty comfort settings: fewer ads, faster menus, no Edge in the background.
win_optimize.about: Around fifty small settings change in one go to make Windows calmer to use. You'll see fewer suggestions and ads, menus open faster, and Edge stops running once you close it. It's about everyday comfort, and your frame rate will rarely change in a way you can measure. Know that it also turns off Windows Remote Assistance and stops syncing your settings and passwords with your Microsoft account.

win_diag.summary: Lets Windows' data collection start only when needed and turns off crash reporting.
win_diag.about: Normally, Windows starts its data collection automatically and sends a report to Microsoft when something crashes. With this on, the data collection part only starts when something calls for it, and crash reporting is switched off. You get a bit more privacy, with no real change in game. If you are trying to figure out why a game or Windows keeps crashing, those missing reports can make it harder.

win_services.summary: Turns off several background Windows features, like printing, and removes the Cortana app.
win_services.about: Several Windows features keep running whether you use them or not. This switches off the scanning that keeps file search fast, along with printing, offline files and crash reporting, and it removes Cortana and an older Copilot component. Fewer things run in the background, though the effect on frames is rarely measurable. It's for players who know they can live without these, since file search gets slower and printing and the notification center stop working.
win_services.undo: Turn it off to bring the features back. The Cortana app stays uninstalled.

win_store.summary: Keeps Windows update sharing to PCs on your local network and leaves the Store on.
win_store.about: Update files can be shared between PCs, and not only those on your own network. This keeps that sharing to the computers on your local network and leaves the Microsoft Store working as usual. In many cases Windows is already set up this way, so you will likely notice no change at all. It's a harmless check with no known downside, mostly for peace of mind.

cln_temp.summary: Deletes the temporary files that Windows and your user account have piled up.
cln_temp.about: Over time, Windows and your user account collect temporary files that are no longer needed. Running this once deletes them and frees up space on your drive. It won't give you more frames, but it's a quick way to get some room back, with no known downside. You can run it again whenever you feel like tidying up.

cln_devices.summary: Clears out old devices Windows still remembers, like USB drives and headsets you unplugged.
cln_devices.about: Windows keeps a record of devices you've plugged in before, like old USB drives or headsets, even once they're gone. This one-time cleanup removes those leftover entries to tidy up the device list. It won't change your frames. If you plug one of them back in, it sets itself up again, though you may need to redo its settings.

cln_disk.summary: Opens the Windows Disk Cleanup tool so you can pick which unneeded files to delete.
cln_disk.about: There's a tool built into Windows for clearing out files you don't need, and this opens it for you. You choose which kinds of files to remove, then it deletes them to free up drive space. It won't give you more frames on its own. Read each checkbox before you confirm, because some, like Downloads, contain your own files.

cln_repair.summary: Checks the Windows system image for damage and repairs it, after clearing out old updates.
cln_repair.about: If Windows crashes or behaves oddly, this is a good thing to try. It first clears out old updates, then checks the stored copy of system files that Windows repairs itself from and fixes any damage it finds. On a healthy PC it won't change your frames. Plan for it to take several minutes, and stay connected to the Internet in case it needs to download repairs.

gpu_nvidia.summary: Applies a full set of low-delay settings to your NVIDIA card for all your games.
gpu_nvidia.about: On NVIDIA cards, this pack sets a low-delay profile for every game, keeps the card at full speed and adjusts other driver settings. It also turns off video copy protection, NVIDIA's data collection and update checks, and deletes leftover installer files. The profile matters most when your graphics card is working flat out, where it can make your aim feel a bit more responsive, while the rest rarely makes a difference you can feel. Your global NVIDIA settings get replaced, Netflix may refuse to play and the card runs warmer even on the desktop.
gpu_nvidia.undo: Turn it off to put back most settings. Your previous NVIDIA profile and the deleted installer files don't come back.

gpu_amd.summary: Sets up your AMD card for lower input delay and steady speed in every game.
gpu_amd.about: For AMD cards, this pack turns off power saving and Chill, keeps the card at high speed, turns on Anti-Lag and adjusts other 3D driver settings. Anti-Lag is the part that can help, making your mouse feel quicker when the card is fully loaded. The rest rarely changes anything you would notice. Expect more heat, fan noise and power use, and because VSync is forced off, some screen tearing can appear.

gpu_intel.summary: Adjusts Intel graphics driver settings for sync, video memory and power use.
gpu_intel.about: On PCs with Intel graphics, this adjusts a few driver settings. Adaptive VSync is turned off, more memory is set aside for video, and the power profile is changed. In practice, recent Intel drivers already manage their video memory well by themselves, so you will rarely see a difference. It has no known drawback, so it's a harmless extra to include if Intel graphics is what runs your games.

gpu_general.summary: Changes a set of Windows graphics settings that work with any graphics card.
gpu_general.about: Whatever graphics card you have, this changes a handful of Windows graphics settings. It gives the display a higher priority, lets the card finish one job before switching to another, changes how the card signals your processor and shortens power-saving delays. Recent versions of Windows ignore many of these settings, so don't expect a visible change. If another app uses the graphics card heavily while you play, the screen can stutter a little.

gpu_directx.summary: Changes old DirectX settings used only by games built on DirectX 7 to 9.
gpu_directx.about: Some older games run on DirectX 7, 8 or 9, and this changes a few graphics settings that only those versions use. Minecraft does not read them, and neither do newer games made with DirectX 11 or 12. For most PvP players, it won't change anything you can see or feel. It only has a chance of mattering if you also play older titles, and since it has no known drawback, leaving it on does no harm.

nv_general.summary: Applies a low-delay profile and several other driver changes to your NVIDIA card.
nv_general.about: Several NVIDIA driver changes come in one package here, led by a low-delay profile for all your games. It also turns off video copy protection and NVIDIA's data collection, among other settings. The profile helps most when your graphics card is fully loaded, and if a game offers NVIDIA Reflex in its own settings, that option does a better job. Keep in mind that Netflix and other streaming video may refuse to play, and your global NVIDIA settings get replaced.
nv_general.undo: Turn it off to put back most settings. Your previous NVIDIA profile doesn't come back.

nv_profile.summary: Loads a low-delay profile into your NVIDIA driver that applies to all your games.
nv_profile.about: Rago's ready-made low-delay profile gets loaded into your NVIDIA driver and applies to every game you play, with no restart needed. It's most useful when your graphics card runs at full load, which is when it can trim the delay between your mouse and the screen. When a game has NVIDIA Reflex in its own settings, turning that on works better. If you have set up your own 3D settings in the NVIDIA Control Panel, note that this profile takes their place.
nv_profile.undo: Turning it off doesn't bring your previous NVIDIA settings back yet.

nv_telemetry.summary: Stops NVIDIA's crash reports, data collection and automatic update checks.
nv_telemetry.about: NVIDIA's software sends crash reports, collects usage data and checks for updates in the background. Turning this on stops all three. It's mainly about privacy and having less going on behind your game, not about frame rate, which stays about the same. The catch is that you may not hear about new drivers anymore, so check NVIDIA's site now and then if you want to stay current.

nv_power.summary: Turns off hidden NVIDIA display power saving and a few Windows power-saving settings.
nv_power.about: The NVIDIA driver and Windows both have power-saving settings that are hidden from the usual menus. This turns off the driver's display power saving along with a few of those Windows options, for players who would rather favor performance than save energy. Windows often ignores several of them, so most players won't notice a difference. On a laptop, expect slightly shorter battery life, and the per-app battery usage list in Windows may lose its details.

nv_pstates.summary: Keeps your NVIDIA card from slowing itself down when it has little to do.
nv_pstates.about: Graphics cards normally slow down when they have little work, then speed back up when a game needs them. With this on, your NVIDIA card stays at its higher speed instead. That can prevent small speed dips during a match, though cards already speed up quickly, so the effect is often small. The card will also stay at full speed on the desktop, which means more heat, fan noise and power use, something laptop players should weigh.

nv_msi.summary: Switches your NVIDIA card to a more modern way of signaling your processor.
nv_msi.about: Your graphics card regularly signals the processor when it needs attention. This switches your NVIDIA card to a newer, more modern way of sending those signals. Recent graphics cards already work this way, so the change mostly matters on older hardware. If your card is a few generations old, it's worth a try, and there's no known drawback.

nv_hdcp.summary: Turns off the copy protection your NVIDIA card uses for streaming video.
nv_hdcp.about: Streaming services like Netflix rely on a copy protection system built into your graphics card, and this turns it off on NVIDIA cards. Games don't use that protection at all, so your frame rate and mouse response stay the same. The trade-off is real, though: protected video may refuse to play or drop to low quality. Only consider it if you never watch streaming services on this PC.

nv_preemption.summary: Makes your NVIDIA card finish each task before switching, instead of pausing it.
nv_preemption.about: Normally your graphics card can pause what it's doing to handle something more urgent, then come back to it. With this on, your NVIDIA card finishes its current task before moving to the next one. In games the difference is rarely measurable, and if another app uses the card heavily, your screen can stutter. Wireless display may also stop working, so leave this to players who know what they're changing.

nv_dpc.summary: Lets the NVIDIA driver spread its small urgent jobs across all your processor cores.
nv_dpc.about: Your NVIDIA driver has small, urgent jobs it hands to the processor, and normally they all go to a single core. This lets them run on any core instead. The idea is to keep one core from getting crowded, but NVIDIA doesn't document this setting and its effect is rarely measurable in practice. With no known drawback, it's an easy one to leave on if you like having everything tuned.

nv_writecomb.summary: Stops Windows from grouping small graphics memory writes together into batches.
nv_writecomb.about: When Windows schedules work for your graphics card, it normally gathers small pieces of data into batches before writing them to memory. This turns that grouping off. Windows often ignores this setting, so you're unlikely to notice any change while playing. It has no known drawback, which makes it a harmless addition for players who want every option covered.

nv_accel.summary: Makes sure your NVIDIA card's hardware acceleration is set to full.
nv_accel.about: Hardware acceleration lets your graphics card take on drawing work instead of leaving it to the processor. This sets it to full on your NVIDIA card. Full is already what Windows uses by default, so on most PCs nothing changes. It mainly acts as a safety net in case the setting was lowered at some point, and it has no known drawback.

nv_contig.summary: Asks the NVIDIA driver to reserve its memory in your RAM as one single block.
nv_contig.about: Part of your PC's memory (RAM) is set aside for the graphics card to use. On NVIDIA cards, this asks the driver to reserve that space as one single block rather than in separate pieces. Very little is documented about this setting, and any effect on your games is rarely measurable. It has no known drawback, so you can leave it on without worry.

nv_debloat.summary: Deletes leftover NVIDIA installer files to free up space on your drive.
nv_debloat.about: Each time you install an NVIDIA driver, its setup files can stay behind on your main drive. This runs once and deletes them, while the driver you already have stays installed and keeps working. It's purely about getting disk space back, so your games run exactly the same. If you ever need to repair or reinstall the driver, you'll just have to download the installer again.

nv_advanced.summary: Changes about forty internal NVIDIA driver and power settings in one go.
nv_advanced.about: For players who like to go deep, this changes about forty internal settings in the NVIDIA driver and its power management. It also turns off NVIDIA's data collection and wireless display support. Most of these settings are undocumented, so any effect on your games is rarely measurable, and it's best left to people who know what they are changing. If you send your screen to a TV or another display without a cable, that may stop working.

nv_powermizer.summary: Sets NVIDIA power management to favor maximum performance over saving energy.
nv_powermizer.about: NVIDIA cards manage their own power, lowering their speed when there's less to do. Setting that management to maximum performance keeps the card at higher speeds more often. The aim is to avoid small speed dips during a game, but on recent drivers it's unclear how much it changes. Your card will run warmer and louder and use more power, which matters most if you play on a laptop.

nv_latency.summary: Shortens how long the NVIDIA driver waits before changing its power-saving state.
nv_latency.about: Before your graphics card switches between power-saving states, the NVIDIA driver waits for a short moment. This shortens those waits, but only on the first graphics card in your PC. On laptops with two graphics chips, that may be the built-in one rather than the NVIDIA card, and the settings themselves are undocumented. In practice the effect is rarely measurable, though there's no known drawback to having it on.

nv_kboost.summary: Locks your NVIDIA card at its maximum speed all the time, even on the desktop.
nv_kboost.about: Instead of speeding up and slowing down with the workload, your NVIDIA card stays at its top speed the whole time your PC is on. That can prevent small speed dips in games. It comes at a cost, though: more heat, fan noise, power use and wear, even while you're just browsing. On laptops it may affect the built-in graphics chip instead, so this one is for experienced players who know what they're turning on.

amd_general.summary: Adjusts AMD driver settings so fewer frames wait in line and textures favor speed.
amd_general.about: This changes several AMD driver settings at once. Fewer frames are allowed to wait in line before reaching your screen, texture quality leans toward speed, and the Radeon overlay and some extra options are turned off. When your graphics card is fully loaded, that can trim a little input lag, though the effect on recent drivers is uncertain. Textures may look slightly less sharp, so it suits players who care more about response than looks.

amd_power.summary: Keeps your AMD card out of its power-saving and deep sleep modes.
amd_power.about: AMD cards have built-in power saving, including a very low-power sleep state for quiet moments. This turns that power saving off, so the card doesn't have to wake up again when a game needs it. The goal is to avoid small hitches at those moments, though the effect is often small. Expect more power use and heat while idle, which counts most on a laptop.

amd_hdcp.summary: Tries to turn off the copy protection your AMD card uses for streaming video.
amd_hdcp.about: On AMD cards, this tries to switch off the copy protection that streaming services use to protect their video. The change is aimed at one specific monitor model, so it most likely won't apply to your setup. Even where it does work, your games run exactly the same, and Netflix or other protected video may refuse to play. For most players, there's little reason to turn it on.

amd_memsleep.summary: Stops your AMD graphics chip from going into deep sleep during quiet moments.
amd_memsleep.about: When it has little to do, your AMD graphics chip can drop into a deep sleep to save energy, and waking it back up takes a moment. This keeps it from going that deep. The idea is to avoid tiny hitches when the chip is suddenly needed again, but the difference is often small. Idle power use and heat go up slightly, so laptop players may want to skip it.

amd_delag.summary: Turns on AMD Anti-Lag so your processor doesn't run too far ahead of your card.
amd_delag.about: Anti-Lag is an AMD driver feature that stops your processor from getting too far ahead of your graphics card. When the card is working at full load, this can shorten the delay between moving your mouse and seeing it on screen. If your card isn't maxed out, it won't change anything. Some games may lose a little FPS with it on, so it's worth checking your frame rate after enabling it.

amd_logging.summary: Turns off the AMD driver's logging, so one less small program runs in the background.
amd_logging.about: Your AMD driver keeps a small logging program running in the background to record what it does. This switches it off, leaving one less thing running alongside your games. The program is tiny, so the effect on performance is rarely measurable. It's mostly a tidiness choice for players who like a lean PC, and there's no known drawback.

amd_advanced.summary: Turns off AMD power saving, keeps the card at high speed and turns on Anti-Lag.
amd_advanced.about: Meant for players who know what they're changing, this pack switches off the AMD card's power saving and Chill, keeps the card at high speed and turns on Anti-Lag, plus other 3D driver settings. Anti-Lag is the part most likely to help, by cutting some input lag when your card is maxed out. The other changes rarely make a measurable difference. Your PC will run hotter and louder and use more power, and with VSync forced off you may see screen tearing.
